steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a conceptual, step-by-step picture of how a Transformer works:

1. Input Representation  
   • Tokens → Embeddings: Each word (or subword) in the input sequence is converted into a fixed-dimensional vector.  
   • Positional Encoding: Since the model has no built-in sense of word order, we add or concatenate a position-dependent vector (often sinusoidal) so the model can tell “this is token #1, this is #2,” etc.

2. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
   • Queries, Keys, Values: For each token embedding, three different linear projections produce a “query” vector Q, a “key” vector K, and a “value” vector V.  
   • Attention Scores: Compute the dot-product Q·Kᵀ (scaled by 1/√d) to measure how much each token should attend to every other.  
   • Softmax Weights: Apply softmax across the scores so they sum to 1—giving a distribution of attention over all positions.  
   • Weighted Sum: Multiply these weights by the V vectors and sum, yielding a new representation for each token that mixes information from the whole sequence.  
   • Multi-Head: Repeat the above in parallel H times with different linear projections. This lets the model capture diverse relationships (syntax, semantics, position, etc.). The H outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

3. Position-Wise Feed-Forward  
   • After attention, each token’s vector passes through the same small feed-forward network (two linear layers with a nonlinearity in between). This adds capacity for more complex transformations.

4. Residual Connections and Layer Normalization  
   • Around each sub-layer (multi-head attention and feed-forward), we add the original input (“residual connection”) and then normalize.  
   • This stabilizes training and helps gradients flow through deep stacks.

5. Stacking Layers  
   • Repeat (multi-head attention → feed-forward) N times. Each layer refines token representations by mixing global context and local transformations.

6. Encoder-Decoder Architecture (for seq2seq tasks)  
   • Encoder: A stack as above processes the source sequence.  
   • Decoder:  
     – Masked Self-Attention: Prevents the decoder from “seeing” future tokens when generating autoregressively.  
     – Cross-Attention: Decoder queries attend to encoder outputs as keys/values, letting it incorporate source information.  
     – Feed-Forward and residual/norm just like the encoder.

7. Final Output  
   • In language generation, each decoder output vector is projected to vocabulary logits and a probability distribution is formed (via softmax). The highest-probability token (or a sample) becomes the next generated word.

Key Benefits  
   • Parallelizable: Unlike RNNs, all positions in a layer are processed simultaneously.  
   • Flexible Context: Any token can attend directly to any other, making it easier to model long-range dependencies.  
   • Scalable: By stacking more layers or heads, you can increase capacity without changing the core mechanism.

In essence, a Transformer learns to “route” information dynamically between all parts of a sequence at every layer, building up richly contextualized representations that power state-of-the-art language, vision, and multimodal models.
